chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Portfolio Thinking Beats Stock Picking

lessons.title: Portfolio Return: The Weighted Average That's Easy to Get Wrong

children.text: You now know how to measure a single stock's expected return and risk. The next question is simple to ask and, it turns out, surprisingly easy to answer wrong: if you own several stocks together, what is your portfolio's return? The formula itself is the easiest piece of math in this entire course. Almost every mistake investors make with it happens before the formula, in how they compute the weights that go into it.

body.text: Portfolio return is a rupee-value-weighted average of the returns of everything you hold. Get the weights right, and the arithmetic is trivial. Get the weights wrong, and a perfectly correct-looking formula hands you a confidently wrong number.

body.caption: Portfolio return is the sum of each holding's weight multiplied by its return. The weights must add up to 1 (100%).

markDefs.definition: The proportion of a portfolio's total rupee value held in a given asset, calculated as that asset's current market value divided by the portfolio's total current market value.

children.text: The weight w_i here is a

: the current rupee value of that holding, divided by the current rupee value of the whole portfolio. Not the number of shares. Not what you paid for it. What it is worth right now, as a share of everything you own right now.
A ₹5,00,000 portfolio held on Zerodha, split across four stocks, returned the following over the last month:

body.caption: Portfolio return, correctly weighted by rupee value (illustrative)

children.text: Each contribution is weight multiplied by return. Add the four contributions, 3.2% + 4.5% - 1.0% + 2.0%, and the portfolio returned 8.7% for the month. That is the entire calculation. What follows is where people go wrong before they ever get here.

body.text: Notice how clean this is: portfolio return is exactly the weighted average of individual returns, no adjustment needed. Portfolio risk does not work this way. Chapter 2 shows that portfolio variance is NOT the weighted average of individual variances, because it also depends on how the holdings move together. Return is the easy half of this course. Risk is the hard half.

children.text: Mistake 1: Weighting by Number of Shares, Not Rupee Value

Share price varies enormously across NSE. A high-priced stock like MRF trades in the tens of thousands of rupees per share, while plenty of small and mid caps trade in double digits. An investor holding 5 shares of an expensive stock and 2,000 shares of a cheap one can look at the share counts and assume the cheap stock dominates the portfolio. It usually does not.

body.title: Same Two Holdings, Two Ways of Weighting Them

columns.label: Naive: weight by share count
points: Stock X: 5 shares, Stock Y: 2,000 shares
"Y has 400 times more shares, so Y must dominate"
Guessed portfolio return: close to Y's -20%

columns.label: Correct: weight by rupee value
points: Stock X: 5 shares x ₹40,000 = ₹2,00,000 (71.4% of portfolio)
Stock Y: 2,000 shares x ₹40 = ₹80,000 (28.6% of portfolio)

body.text: The naive guess and the correct answer are not close. Guessing -20% when the real number is +1.43% is not a rounding error, it is a completely wrong read on the portfolio, purely because share count was mistaken for rupee weight.

children.text: Mistake 2: Weights That Don't Sum to 100%

A common version of this mistake is forgetting a cash or liquid-fund sleeve entirely. Suppose a ₹6,00,000 portfolio holds Stock A worth ₹3,00,000 (return 12%) and Stock B worth ₹2,00,000 (return 6%), with the remaining ₹1,00,000 sitting in a liquid fund earning 3.5%. An investor who only looks at the two stocks and weights them against each other, ignoring the cash, computes weights of 60% and 40% instead of the true 50%, 33.3%, and 16.7% across all three holdings.

stats.label: Wrong (cash ignored)
stats.context: (0.60 x 12%) + (0.40 x 6%), only two holdings weighted

stats.label: Overstatement
stats.context: A small but real, systematic error

children.text: Every rupee in the portfolio needs a weight, including cash, and every weight needs to be accounted for. If your weights do not sum to 100% before you start multiplying, stop and find the missing piece before you trust the answer.
Mistake 3: Using Stale Weights After Prices Have Moved

Six months ago, an investor split ₹2,00,000 equally between Stock A and Stock B, ₹1,00,000 each, a 50/50 weight. Since then, Stock A is up 60% to ₹1,60,000, and Stock B is down 20% to ₹80,000. The portfolio is now worth ₹2,40,000, and the true current weights are 66.7% in A and 33.3% in B. If the investor now wants to estimate next month's expected portfolio return, using A's expected return of 2% and B's expected return of 15%, the weights they use matter enormously.

body.caption: Stale weights vs current weights, same expected returns

body.text: Weights drift automatically as prices move, with no trading required. A position that outperforms silently grows into a bigger share of the book, and one that underperforms silently shrinks. Any forward-looking calculation, expected return, risk, or otherwise, needs today's weights, not the weights from whenever the position was first built. This is also the mechanical reason rebalancing exists, covered in Chapter 6.

children.text: A Note for Anyone Who Shorts

The formula does not change for a short position, only the sign of its weight does. If a ₹5,00,000 book carries a ₹50,000 short position, that position's weight is -10%, and it plugs into the same sum: multiply the negative weight by that position's return, exactly like a long position. Weights across a book with shorts and leverage do not have to be positive fractions between 0 and 1, but they still have to sum to 1 in total, once every long, short, and cash position is included.

body.title: Weight the book, then compute the return
body.prompt: A portfolio holds Stock P worth ₹3,00,000 (return +9%), Stock Q worth ₹1,50,000 (return -4%), and Stock R worth ₹1,50,000 (return +18%). What is the portfolio's return for the period?

body.title: Spot the mistake
body.question: An investor holds Stock M worth ₹4,00,000 (expected return 6%) and Stock N worth ₹1,00,000 (expected return 20%). He computes the portfolio's expected return using 50% and 50% weights, reasoning that he owns "two stocks." What is he getting wrong?
options: Nothing, 50/50 is correct whenever a portfolio holds exactly two stocks
He should be using each stock's historical return instead of its expected return
He is treating equal stock count as equal weight, when the true rupee split is 80% M and 20% N
He forgot to include a cash allocation
body.explanation: The correct weights are ₹4,00,000 / ₹5,00,000 = 80% for M and ₹1,00,000 / ₹5,00,000 = 20% for N. The correct expected return is (0.8 x 6%) + (0.2 x 20%) = 4.8% + 4.0% = 8.8%, well below his wrong 50/50 estimate of (0.5 x 6%) + (0.5 x 20%) = 13%.

cards.definition: An asset's current rupee value divided by the portfolio's total current rupee value. Not share count, not original cost.
The sum of each holding's weight multiplied by its own return, R_p = sum of w_i times R_i.
The automatic change in a holding's portfolio weight as prices move, even with no buying or selling.
A negative portfolio weight, used for a shorted asset, that plugs into the same weighted-return formula as any long position.

points: Portfolio return is a rupee-value-weighted average of individual returns. The formula itself is exact and never needs adjustment.
Weights come from current market value, never from share count and never from original purchase cost.
Every rupee in the portfolio, including cash and liquid funds, needs a weight. If the weights don't sum to 100%, the calculation is wrong before it starts.
Weights drift automatically as prices move. A forward-looking calculation needs today's weights, not the weights from when the position was first built.
A short position simply carries a negative weight in the same formula; the mechanics do not change.
Unlike return, portfolio risk is NOT a simple weighted average of individual risks. That is the subject of the next chapter.
